items_missed: Move date never asked and availability never checked - the call ends without a date on the table
No agenda statement - 'You have a few minutes to talk it over' is a permission ask, not 'here's what we'll do and how long'
Zip codes never confirmed at either end; special considerations asked only at the destination, never at the origin
'No hidden fees' given as a general claim, not the itemized pitch (no credit card fees, no transportation fees, no fuel surcharge, no assembly fees)
Two-story destination never named as an estimate variable despite the customer volunteering it
No equivalents/analogy (school bus reference or similar) to make the time range land
Entire Save Your Ass prep speech absent - no consolidation examples, no carload tip, no 'does that make sense' close; only a passing nod to the customer's own trailer plan
No attempt to set on schedule today, and no attempt to book the virtual walkthrough he himself said was required
No deposit required never mentioned - the single strongest objection-killer against a customer who is actively shopping
Email handoff never explained - no confirmation email promised, no BOLDED key-details list, no 'reply with any corrections'
No closing 'any other questions before I let you go?'
Customer's name used twice, both in the opening line
top_strength: The differentiator block is the best work on this call and it visibly moved the customer - she went from flat 'Okay's to 'Oh, that's wonderful' and 'no, no questions are fantastic.' Joel hit all three differentiators cleanly, and his insurance explanation is the standout: rather than just naming No Worries, he set it against the industry baseline with a concrete example - 'the majority of them offers 60 cents per pound... let's just say they were to damage your TV... they'll end up paying like $20 to $30 to settle that TV claim which is nowhere near the value of that item.' He then stacked credibility on top of it without sounding boastful ('we don't hire dai labors, no contract workers none of that, they're all full-time employees') and checked in twice with 'Any questions there?' instead of monologuing straight through. His intake was thorough and his estimate math was honest - when she pushed back with a hypothetical three hours, he answered the real number ('three hours comes out to about 1400') instead of dodging.
coaching_note: He earned the sale and then never asked for it. The customer told him she was in-market right now - 'We're still kind of shopping around a little bit. We just started looking around today' - and asked point-blank how to book: 'do I just call you back or do I go online?' That is the softest close in the business, and Joel handed it back to her: 'Yeah, either, either option you can give us a call or or reply back to the email and and we can go from there.' He also told her a virtual walkthrough was necessary to right-size the crew, then never scheduled it. The fix is one sentence at that exact moment: 'There's no deposit to book, so let's put your date on the calendar and get that virtual walkthrough scheduled now - if anything changes we'll adjust.' He never asked her move date either, so he had nothing to hold. Second miss, worth real money: she volunteered 'we're also gonna move some stuff beforehand cause we have a trailer' - a perfect opening for the Save Your Ass speech, which on a 6.5-hour job at $96 per mover per hour could take hundreds off her bill and tighten the estimate at the same time. He let it pass with a nod instead of coaching her on consolidating drawers, toys, and carload items.
phone_presence_notes: Polite and professional with real moments of warmth ('Doing well, thanks for asking') and a customer who ended up genuinely pleased, but the warmth is procedural - her name appears only in the opening line, acknowledgments are a repeating 'Okay. Cool,' and the middle of the call is a long scripted differentiator monologue rather than a back-and-forth.
